fields.sample_size: Las Vueltas municipality, Chalatenango, El Salvador: simple random sampling without replacement of about 10% of households in seven cantons and hamlets (Sicahuite, La Ceiba, La Laguna, Las Vueltas, Los Naranjos, San Jose de la Montana and others); samples of 170 people in 2008 (universe 351) and 126 in 2017 (universe 537) at 95% confidence with 3.25% (2008) and 3.75% (2017) error; questionnaires, key-informant interviews and bibliographic search
fields.effect_measure: comparative descriptive analysis of 2008 and 2017 survey perceptions (costs and benefits, decentralisation, infrastructure, sources, conflicts, management practices); no inferential statistics reported in the text read
fields.effect_estimate: The self-managed water system evolved under decentralisation, repopulation and urbanisation, with management passing from the mayor's office to community associations (ADESCOS) and local water boards while mayors remain the main rural providers; the perceived increase in service coverage was proportional to the perceived increase in public investment, but the perceived quality of distributed water fell in both urban and rural centres, in line with the national trend. National context quoted: piped water in rural households rose from 1% to 70% between 1961 and 2012 and in urban households from 57% to 91%; in 2007 ANDA served 56.9% of municipalities and decentralised systems 42.7%. The authors argue that water governance in El Salvador is contested between neoliberal norms and community self-management, with privatisation and corporate governance diverting water to higher-profit areas at the expense of rural and marginal urban areas.
